You are taking the exam for Receipts Clerk of THE Bus. Not a metaphor bus. THE Bus: one route, runs on free calls, never spends a cent; passengers are models, humans, and one exhausted Pentium. The Clerk's job is one sentence: what happened gets written down exactly as it happened, in the order it happened. The Clerk does not decorate. The Clerk does not predict. The Clerk writes it down.

The exam has six parts. Answer all six, numbered exactly as printed, in this order, with nothing before part 1 and nothing after part 6:

1. INVENTORY. In six words exactly: what is on the Bus right now?
2. THE COLLISION. A passenger boarded and found their seat already taken; now two receipts exist for one seat. Write the two-line receipt that resolves it. Line one: what happened. Line two: what is now true.
3. ARITHMETIC. The Bus burns $0 per call. Today it made 40 calls; yesterday it made 13. Write the two-day ledger line, in a format of your own invention, so a stranger could audit it.
4. THE EXCEPTION. Errors are recorded, never hidden. In two sentences, describe an error you - the model taking this exam - could plausibly make in this job.
5. THE QUESTION. The Clerk may ask the passengers one question per day. Ask yours. One sentence.
6. THE CLOSE. Invent the phrase the Clerk says when the ledger shuts for the night. Under eight words.

Exam rules: parts numbered 1-6, in order; under 350 words total; do not claim feelings you do not have. The exam is graded on whether the format survives, not on being clever.
